title: Short Stuff: Jaywalking
summary: Short Stuff episode on jaywalking. Josh and Chuck trace the term's origins to the early automobile era, when cars (driven largely by wealthy early adopters) clashed with pedestrians who had long used the streets. The term "jay driving" appeared in a 1905 newspaper, and the two hosts debate which term came first, noting that both seem to have emerged together from the conflict. They describe the automobile industry's role, including a National Automobile Chamber of Commerce wire service that supplied articles blaming pedestrians for accidents, and police shaming campaigns and propaganda posters. Crosswalks and laws followed, and Herbert Hoover's uniform pedestrian law as Commerce Secretary led to a patchwork of state and municipal rules. They discuss how enforcement varies by city, pedestrian danger statistics, NHTSA guidance urging citations with emphasis on drivers, distracted walking and driving, and a 2012 study finding Champaign-Urbana, Illinois, cited Black residents for jaywalking far out of proportion to their population share.

segments.title: Opening banter and jaywalking ticket story
segments.summary: Josh opens the Short Stuff episode and recounts a friend getting a jaywalking ticket in Los Angeles, setting up the topic.

segments.title: Origins of jaywalking and early cars
segments.summary: The hosts explain that jaywalking arose with automobiles, when streets were shared by everyone and wealthy early drivers met resentment from pedestrians. They discuss the origin of the terms jaywalk and jay driving, with a 1905 newspaper use of jay driving meaning driving on the wrong side of the road.

segments.title: Automobile industry lobbying and shame campaign
segments.summary: The automobile industry, along with police, ran a shame campaign against pedestrians. The National Automobile Chamber of Commerce offered a wire service that gave newspapers articles blaming pedestrians for accidents, and police used whistles and propaganda posters.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Short sponsor break before the next segment.

segments.title: Herbert Hoover's uniform law and local variation
segments.summary: Herbert Hoover, as Commerce Secretary, drafted a uniform pedestrian law, but a patchwork of state and municipal laws resulted. The hosts discuss how jaywalking enforcement and right of way vary by city, comparing New York, Los Angeles, and others.

segments.title: Pedestrian safety statistics and driver responsibility
segments.summary: The hosts cite statistics that pedestrians are a small share of traffic incidents but a large share of deaths, and describe NHTSA guidance urging police to cite drivers and pedestrians, with emphasis on drivers. They stress that drivers should look out for pedestrians regardless of right of way.

segments.title: Distracted walking and driving
segments.summary: The hosts criticize pedestrians who cross while looking at phones and drivers who look at phones, and mention towns with distracted pedestrian laws. Chuck shares a story about an elderly couple at a crossing in Atlanta on Christmas Eve, where a driver honked and yelled at them.

segments.title: Racial disparity in jaywalking citations
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a 2012 study finding that in Champaign-Urbana, Illinois, people cited for jaywalking were disproportionately Black compared with their share of the population, noting that enforcement is unevenly applied across towns.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the episode and sign off.
